en: Feeds your people. Every pop eats food each month, and only a surplus lets a colony grow.
The currency of the frontier. It pays the upkeep of districts, buildings, fleets and beacons, and buys goods on the market.
Stone and ore. Spent on districts, buildings and ships, and refined into alloys.
Refined metal for hulls, starbases, beacons and great projects.
Insight from researchers and anomalies. It flows into the tech cards you are studying in physics, society and engineering.
Political capital. Spent on outposts, claims, treaties, edicts and hard choices.
Terraced homes, commons and a clerk's office. It adds housing, a little energy and a little calm.
Fields and greenhouses worked by farmers. Farms next to other farms share water and machinery.
Solar fields, fusion cells and the technicians who run them.
Pits and shafts worked by miners. Industry built next door gets its ore cheaper.
Smelters that turn minerals into alloys. Their smoke unsettles nearby homes.
Laboratories staffed by researchers in the branch you choose. They run better next to a reliable power supply.
Oceans, continents and weather that people can live in without a dome. Rare, and worth a great deal.
Nearly all water. Fisheries and kelp farms make it generous with food.
Dry, bright and rich in minerals. Livable, if you do not mind the dust.
A frozen crust over dark water. Only domed settlements survive, but the cold suits delicate instruments.
Airless rock. Domes only; the ground itself is the prize.
A poisonous sky full of restless chemistry. Domes only; the reactions can be tapped for energy.
No surface to stand on. Orbital outposts can skim energy or study the storms.
A ring of rubble around the star. Outposts only, for minerals.
Deep living soil left by an older climate. Farm districts here yield more.
Ore close to the surface. Mining districts here yield more.
Heat rises from the mantle. Energy districts here yield more.
One face always burns and the other always freezes. Less room to build, strong sunlight, uneasy people.
The air would kill you. Settle under domes only; industry thrives on the chemistry.
Light footsteps and cheap launches. Alloys come easier and ships built here cost less.
Something was built here long before us. One slot stays blocked until the ruins are surveyed.
Charged particles sing through the magnetosphere. Good for research, hard on the nerves.
Descendants of the generation ark that settled Ember a century ago. Cohesive, patient, and short of almost everything.
A human successor state grown from the Meridian beacon-keepers, who kept more of Sol's technology than anyone else. Orderly, ambitious, and sure it is Earth's rightful heir.
Long-lived colonial organisms who speak in modulated light. Patient, cautious and courteous, and convinced that humans are dangerously loud.
Descendants of beacon crews stranded when the network went dark. They raid lanes and demand tolls, but they can be paid, hired or beaten.
A large, close-knit people who crossed the dark in one great ship. The Ark's archive holds a sealed order from Sol that no one can open.
Founded as a company venture: good at trade and energy, restless under rule. The parent company may still exist, and may still want its dividends.
Sent away with their warships and without their records. Strong in battle, and unsure who exiled them, or why.
Explorers first and settlers second. The mission's true target was a beacon Sol never admitted to building.
Year 100 of the Silence. Grow the Ark's colonies at Ember and open the sealed order.
Refit the slowboats, cross the dark lanes, face the Unlit, and wake the beacon at Halden's Gate.
Meet the Meridian Directorate and the Vael, and learn what the Vael heard.

Steward Anneliese Varga stands on an upturned seed crate in the Ark's old cargo hall, three hundred faces turned up to her. "We have run this colony by habit for a century," she says. "Habit is not a constitution." Archivist Imre Sola, footnoting as always, reminds everyone that the Ark's charter lapsed the day the relay went quiet. The assembly wants a vote before the harvest. How should Ember govern itself?
Uncertain: either faster research, or a restless decade

Archivist Imre Sola lays the Ark's oldest case on the table: a Sol seal, unbroken for a century. The lock answers to no key the Ark ever carried. "It is addressed to whoever leads," Sola says. "That, I am afraid, is you."
A calm orange star, home for a century. Five worlds circle it; one is settled so far.
Beacon lanes shimmer gold on the map.
